title: Explain costing and the viability of an agri-business

lessons.title: Types of costs on the farm
lessons.html:
Why costing matters

Costing means working out what it costs to produce something. Without knowing costs, a farm cannot tell whether an enterprise makes money, what price is acceptable, or where to save.

Variable costs

Variable (direct) costs change with the size of production. If you plant more hectares or keep more animals, they go up. Examples:

  • Seed, fertiliser, lime and chemicals
  • Feed, licks, vaccines and dips
  • Fuel and repairs for field work
  • Packaging, transport and marketing commission
  • Casual and seasonal labour

Fixed costs

Fixed (overhead) costs stay roughly the same whether production is big or small, at least in the short term. Examples:

  • Permanent salaries
  • Depreciation of tractors, bakkies and buildings
  • Insurance, rates and licence fees
  • Interest on long-term loans
  • Office, telephone and accounting costs

Depreciation

Machinery loses value as it ages. Depreciation spreads the purchase cost over the useful life. A simple straight-line method: (purchase price minus estimated value at end of life) divided by years of use. For example, a tractor bought for R800 000, worth R200 000 after 10 years, depreciates by R60 000 per year.

Total cost and cost per unit

Total cost = variable costs + fixed costs. Cost per unit = total cost divided by units produced. If a maize land costs R180 000 in total and yields 60 tonnes, the cost is R3 000 per tonne.

Knowing cost per unit lets the farm compare it with the market price. If the price is below cost per unit, each tonne sold loses money.

lessons.title: Gross margin, break-even and viability
lessons.html:
Gross margin

Gross margin = gross income minus variable costs. It shows how much an enterprise contributes towards fixed costs and profit, and it is the usual way to compare enterprises on a farm.

Example: 10 ha cabbageRand
Gross income (sales)R450 000
Variable costs (seedlings, fertiliser, sprays, labour, packaging, transport)R310 000
Gross marginR140 000
Gross margin per hectareR14 000

Net profit

Net farm profit = total gross margin of all enterprises minus fixed costs. A farm can have positive gross margins but still make a loss if fixed costs are too high.

Break-even

The break-even point is where income equals total costs. Two useful forms:

  • Break-even price = total cost divided by expected yield. This is the lowest price the farm can accept without a loss.
  • Break-even yield = total cost divided by expected price. This is the minimum yield needed.

Viability

An agri-business is viable when it can, over time:

  • Cover all its costs, including depreciation and interest
  • Pay its debts when they fall due (cash flow)
  • Provide a reasonable return for the owner's capital and management
  • Survive bad seasons, using reserves or diversified income

Improving viability

  • Increase yield or quality with the same inputs.
  • Reduce waste and losses, e.g. bruising, mortalities, theft.
  • Negotiate better input prices or bulk buy with neighbours.
  • Find better markets or add value.
  • Drop or change enterprises with poor margins.

Supervisors contribute by keeping accurate records of inputs used, hours worked and output, because costing is only as good as the data.

Key points

  • Variable costs change with production; fixed costs do not in the short term.
  • Gross margin = income minus variable costs.
  • Net profit = total gross margin minus fixed costs.
  • Break-even price = total cost divided by yield.
  • Viability means covering costs, paying debts and surviving bad seasons.
